title: Newton's Law of Cooling
short_intro: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat of a body is directly proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings. It is an approximate consequence of Stefan-Boltzmann law applicable for small temperature excesses.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct numerical calculations involving cooling time, average temperature method, and temperature versus time graphs.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential equation formulation, exponential temperature decay, and connection with Stefan-Boltzmann law of radiation.

prerequisites: Modes of heat transfer: Conduction, Convection, and Radiation
Specific heat capacity and thermal capacity

concept_notes.heading: Physical Basis of Newton's Law of Cooling
bullets: The law is derived from Stefan-Boltzmann law of radiation under the condition that the temperature difference between the body and surroundings is small.
It assumes that the loss of heat is solely due to radiation and that forced convection conditions or surrounding temperature remain strictly constant.
The rate of cooling depends on the nature of the radiating surface (emissivity) and the total surface area exposed.

concept_notes.heading: Mathematical Formulation
bullets: Let a body of mass m, specific heat s, and surface area A be at temperature T, while the surrounding medium is at constant temperature T_0.
The rate of heat loss dQ/dt is proportional to (T - T_0), leading to dQ/dt = -K(T - T_0), where K is a positive constant.
Since dQ = ms dT, the rate of fall of temperature is given by dT/dt = -k(T - T_0), where k = K/(ms).

concept_notes.heading: Average Temperature Method in Numerical Problems
bullets: For moderate temperature differences, the rate of cooling dT/dt can be approximated as the change in temperature divided by time interval: (T_1 - T_2)/t = k(bar{T} - T_0).
Here, bar{T} = (T_1 + T_2)/2 represents the mean temperature of the body during the time interval t.
This approximation is extensively used in UP TGT/PGT examinations to bypass complex exponential integration.

concept_notes.heading: Exponential Decay of Temperature
bullets: Integrating the differential equation dT/dt = -k(T - T_0) yields T(t) = T_0 + (T_i - T_0)e^{-kt}, showing an exponential approach to ambient temperature.
The temperature of the body theoretically reaches the ambient temperature only as time approaches infinity.
The time constant of the cooling process is tau = 1/k, which signifies the time required for the excess temperature to reduce to 1/e of its initial value.

derivations.title: Derivation of Exponential Temperature Decay
derivations.conditions: Small temperature difference between body and surroundings, constant ambient temperature.
steps: Write the fundamental differential equation for temperature decay: \frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_0).
Separate the variables T and t: \frac{dT}{T - T_0} = -k dt.
Integrate both sides with initial condition T = T_i at t = 0: \int_{T_i}^{T} \frac{dT}{T - T_0} = -k \int_{0}^{t} dt.
Exponentiate both sides to obtain the final explicit temperature function.

derivations.title: Approximation of Newton's Law from Stefan-Boltzmann Law
derivations.conditions: Body temperature T is slightly greater than surrounding temperature T_0 (i.e., T - T_0 \ll T_0).
steps: According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, net rate of heat loss is \frac{dQ}{dt} = \sigma A e (T^4 - T_0^4).
Factor the temperature term: T^4 - T_0^4 = (T^2 - T_0^2)(T^2 + T_0^2) = (T - T_0)(T + T_0)(T^2 + T_0^2).
Substitute T \approx T_0 into the binomial sum terms: T^4 - T_0^4 \approx (T - T_0)(2T_0)(2T_0^2) = 4T_0^3(T - T_0).
Substitute back into the radiation equation: \frac{dQ}{dt} = 4 \sigma A e T_0^3 (T - T_0).
Since dQ = ms dT, the cooling rate becomes proportional to (T - T_0) with proportionality constant K = 4 \sigma A e T_0^3 / (ms).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Temperature versus Time Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponential decay curve starting at T_i and asymptotically approaching the horizontal asymptote T = T_0 as t increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the tangent at any point represents the rate of cooling dT/dt at that specific instant, which continuously decreases as the body cools.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in identifying correct qualitative shapes of cooling curves versus heating curves.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Logarithm of Temperature Excess versus Time
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line with a negative slope on a semi-logarithmic plot of \ln(T - T_0) versus t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line equals -k, confirming the exponential nature of Newton's law of cooling.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to determine the experimental cooling constant k from laboratory data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rate of Cooling versus Temperature Difference
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a plot of dT/dt against (T - T_0).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The direct proportionality between the rate of cooling and the temperature excess is verified by the constant linear slope k.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions to check validity limits of linear cooling.

solved_numericals.question: A body cools from 80 \textdegree C to 50 \textdegree C in 5 minutes. Calculate the time it takes to cool from 60 \textdegree C to 30 \textdegree C, if the room temperature is 20 \textdegree C.
solution_steps: Use the average temperature formula: \frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k \left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right).
For the first case: \frac{80 - 50}{5} = k \left(\frac{80 + 50}{2} - 20\right) \implies \frac{30}{5} = k (65 - 20) \implies 6 = k(45) \implies k = \frac{6}{45} = \frac{2}{15} \text{ min}^{-1}.

For the second case, cooling from 60 \textdegree C to 30 \textdegree C in time t: \frac{60 - 30}{t} = k \left(\frac{60 + 30}{2} - 20\right) \implies \frac{30}{t} = \frac{2}{15}(45 - 20) \implies \frac{30}{t} = \frac{2}{15}(25) = \frac{10}{3}.

solved_numericals.question: A liquid cools from 70 \textdegree C to 60 \textdegree C in 5 minutes. The surrounding temperature is 30 \textdegree C. Find the temperature of the liquid after the next 5 minutes.
solution_steps: Apply the average temperature formula for the first interval (70 to 60 \textdegree C): \frac{70 - 60}{5} = k \left(\frac{70 + 60}{2} - 30\right) \implies 2 = k(65 - 30) \implies 2 = k(35) \implies k = \frac{2}{35} \text{ min}^{-1}.
Let the temperature after the next 5 minutes be T. For the second interval (60 to T \textdegree C in 5 minutes): \frac{60 - T}{5} = k \left(\frac{60 + T}{2} - 30\right).
Simplify and solve for T: 7(60 - T) = T \implies 420 - 7T = T \implies 8T = 420 \implies T = \frac{420}{8} = 52.5 \text{ \textdegree C}.

solved_numericals.question: A metal sphere cools from 60 \textdegree C to 50 \textdegree C in 10 minutes. If the room temperature is 25 \textdegree C, what will be its temperature after another 10 minutes?
solution_steps: First interval: average temperature = (60 + 50)/2 = 55 \textdegree C. Temperature excess = 55 - 25 = 30 \textdegree C. Rate of fall = (60 - 50)/10 = 1 \textdegree C/min. Therefore, 1 = k(30) \implies k = 1/30 \text{ min}^{-1}.
Second interval: let final temperature be T after another 10 minutes (cooling from 50 \textdegree C to T \textdegree C).
Average temperature = (50 + T)/2. Excess temperature = (50 + T)/2 - 25 = T/2.
Cross multiply: 6(50 - T) = T \implies 300 - 6T = T \implies 7T = 300 \implies T = \frac{300}{7} \approx 42.86 \text{ \textdegree C}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The temperature difference between the body and surroundings must be small (typically less than 20 \textdegree C to 30 \textdegree C) for the linear approximation to hold accurately.
Heat loss is assumed to occur purely by radiation under uniform convective conditions; forced drafts or varying ambient temperatures invalidate the simple constant k assumption.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Newton's law of cooling applies for any arbitrary large temperature difference.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is valid only for small temperature differences; for large differences, the full Stefan-Boltzmann radiation law must be used.
common_misconceptions.why: Linearization of T^4 - T_0^4 is valid via binomial expansion only when (T - T_0) \ll T_0.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Equal drops in temperature take equal intervals of time.
common_misconceptions.correct: Equal drops in temperature take increasingly longer time intervals as the body approaches room temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: The rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature excess, which decreases exponentially with time.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A body cools at a constant rate throughout its cooling cycle.
common_misconceptions.correct: The cooling rate decreases continuously as the body's temperature drops towards the ambient temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: The driving force for cooling is the temperature difference (T - T_0), which decreases monotonically.

quick_revision: Newton's law of cooling states that dT/dt = -k(T - T_0), implying exponential temperature decay towards the ambient temperature T_0.
Average Temperature Form: \frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k\left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)
